facts: Trans-Neptunian objects, or TNOs, are Solar System bodies that orbit the Sun beyond Neptune.
Neptune orbits the Sun at an average distance of about 30 astronomical units.
One astronomical unit is the average distance between Earth and the Sun.
Most known objects beyond Neptune are found in the Kuiper Belt.
The Kuiper Belt is a broad ring of icy bodies extending roughly from 30 to 50 astronomical units.
Objects past Neptune are considered remnants of the early Solar System.
Because objects past Neptune formed far from the Sun, they preserve clues about primordial Solar System material.
Objects past Neptune are generally much colder than objects in the inner Solar System.
Typical surface temperatures for many objects past Neptune are only a few tens of kelvin above absolute zero.
Objects past Neptune are made largely of mixtures of rock and volatile ices.
Common surface ices on objects past Neptune include water ice.
Methane ice is found on some large objects past Neptune.
Methanol is suspected or detected on the surfaces of some objects past Neptune.
Nitrogen ice is present on Pluto and likely on some other large icy bodies.
Carbon monoxide can also exist as an ice on some outer Solar System bodies.
Objects beyond Neptune fall into several dynamical classes.
Classical Kuiper Belt objects orbit in relatively stable paths beyond Neptune.
Resonant objects past Neptune are locked in orbital resonances with Neptune.
Scattered disk objects follow more eccentric and dynamically excited orbits.
Detached objects orbit far enough away that Neptune no longer strongly controls their present motion.
Pluto is one of the best-known objects past Neptune.
Pluto is a dwarf planet.
Pluto is in a 3:2 orbital resonance with Neptune.
Objects in the same 3:2 resonance are often called plutinos.
Neptune completes three orbits around the Sun in the same time Pluto completes two.
This resonance helps keep Pluto from colliding with Neptune.
Eris is another dwarf planet in the trans-Neptunian region.
Eris is slightly smaller than Pluto but more massive.
Haumea is a rapidly rotating dwarf planet in the trans-Neptunian region.
Haumea's fast rotation gives it an elongated shape.
Haumea is associated with a collisional family of related icy bodies.
Makemake is another large dwarf planet in the Kuiper Belt.
Quaoar is a large object, about half the size of Pluto, with evidence of surface ice.
Sedna follows a very distant and unusual orbit.
Sedna is often discussed as a detached or inner Oort Cloud-like object.
Objects past Neptune can have moons.
Pluto's largest moon is Charon.
Pluto and Charon form a binary-like system because their barycenter lies outside Pluto.
Some objects past Neptune rotate quickly, while others rotate slowly.
Light curves help astronomers measure the rotation periods of objects past Neptune.
Changes in brightness can reveal shape or surface variations.
Some objects past Neptune are very dark and reflect little sunlight.
Some objects past Neptune are brighter because of fresh or reflective surface ices.
Objects past Neptune range in colour from relatively neutral to very red.
Very red objects past Neptune may contain complex organic materials altered by radiation.
These complex reddish materials are often called tholins.
Space weathering changes surfaces of objects past Neptune over time.
Cosmic rays and solar radiation can chemically modify surface ices.
Impacts can also refresh or alter surfaces of objects past Neptune.
Objects past Neptune are important for testing models of planetary migration.
The current structure of the Kuiper Belt suggests the giant planets did not always stay where they are now.
Neptune likely migrated outward early in Solar System history.
That migration helped shape the distribution of objects beyond Neptune's orbit.
Resonant populations of objects past Neptune are strong evidence for Neptune's migration.
The cold classical Kuiper Belt is a particularly important population of objects beyond Neptune.
Cold classical objects past Neptune tend to have low inclinations and relatively undisturbed orbits.
Cold classical objects past Neptune are thought to preserve especially ancient Solar System conditions.
Many cold classical objects are notably red.
Some objects past Neptune may have formed closer to the Sun and later been scattered outward.
Other objects past Neptune may have formed roughly near where they are found today.
Studying objects past Neptune helps astronomers understand where volatile materials were stored in the young Solar System.
SPHEREx is a NASA space telescope designed to survey the entire sky.
SPHEREx stands for Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization, and Ices Explorer.
SPHEREx observes in the near-infrared.
Its spectral coverage spans roughly 0.75 to 5 microns.
SPHEREx collects low-resolution spectra rather than broad-band images alone.
That makes SPHEREx especially useful for identifying surface materials from their spectral signatures.
Ices have diagnostic absorption features in the near-infrared.
Water ice has prominent absorption bands near 1.5 and 2.0 microns.
Water-related features also appear near 3 microns.
Methane ice has characteristic near-infrared absorption features.
Methanol also produces identifiable near-infrared spectral features.
SPHEREx can help distinguish between objects past Neptune with different surface compositions.
A SPHEREx data visualizer could compare spectra of objects past Neptune directly across many objects.
Spectral slopes from SPHEREx data can help quantify how red or neutral an object's surface is.
Combining orbital data with SPHEREx spectral information can improve the taxonomy of objects past Neptune.
SPHEREx can provide uniform observations across large samples of outer Solar System bodies.
Uniform datasets are valuable because they reduce biases from mixing many different instruments.
SPHEREx can help identify broad compositional trends across populations of objects past Neptune.
Those trends may differ between classical, resonant, scattered, and detached objects.
Large objects past Neptune are more likely to retain volatile ices than small ones.
Surface gravity affects whether objects past Neptune can hold onto volatile materials.
Objects like Pluto and Eris retain volatile ices better than many smaller Kuiper Belt objects.
Binary objects past Neptune are common enough to be a major topic in outer Solar System studies.
Binary systems help astronomers measure the masses of objects past Neptune.
Once astronomers know mass and size, they can estimate density.
Density provides clues about the rock-to-ice ratio inside objects past Neptune.
Some objects past Neptune appear ice-rich, while others appear denser and more rock-rich.
Occultations are another powerful method for studying objects past Neptune.
In an occultation, an object past Neptune passes in front of a distant star and briefly blocks its light.
Occultations can measure the sizes of objects past Neptune very accurately.
Occultations can also reveal rings or thin atmospheres around distant bodies.
Pluto has a tenuous, nitrogen-dominated atmosphere.
Pluto's atmosphere changes as it orbits the Sun.
Not all objects past Neptune are spherical; many smaller ones are irregularly shaped.
The farther an object past Neptune is from the Sun, the fainter it usually appears.
That faintness makes all-sky infrared spectral surveys especially valuable.
A SPHEREx-focused visualizer for objects past Neptune could show orbit class, colour, albedo, and spectral ice signatures together.
Combining SPHEREx spectra with dynamical classifications can reveal how composition relates to Solar System history.
Objects beyond Neptune are among the best for studying the frozen, ancient outer Solar System, and SPHEREx is well suited to map their surface compositions at scale.
